holding_summary: Subdivision property owners sought to enjoin defendants from building a tourist court on their lots based on a title restriction against commercial property. The court held the restriction against commercial property was a personal covenant between the original vendor and a predecessor in title, not a covenant running with the land, and therefore did not bind or restrain the defendants' construction of the tourist court (though a separate building-line restriction was enforced).

quotes.text: In our opinion, however, a casual reading of this restriction indicates that it is not a covenant running with the land, but is a personal covenant between the vendor, Claiborne Avenue Extension Realty Company, Inc., and Henry M. Rahders, the predecessor in title of defendants.
it is not a covenant running with the land, but is a personal covenant

notes: No characterization of an actual letting arrangement occurs; case adjudicates enforceability of a covenant restricting construction of a tourist court, effectively permitting the commercial lodging use to proceed. who_was_letting/duration are unclear because no tenants/guests are at issue, only prospective construction of the tourist court itself.

notes: Son was a free family guest, not a paying lodger; the inn-guest comparison is dicta on transience for lien-exemption purposes, unrelated to compensated occupancy.

court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit
holding_summary: In a dispute over the scope of a grantor's reserved lifetime 'use and habitation' of a house conveyed to her nephew, the court held that the codal right of habitation is limited to the necessities of the grantee and her family, but expressly does not prevent the holder of a habitation right from receiving boarders in the house so long as she inhabits it herself.

quotes.text: But nothing prevents him, who enjoys the right of habitation, from receiving in the house, or the part of it which has been assigned to him, friends, guests, or even boarders, provided he inhabits it himself.

The quoted codal provisions, in our opinion, clearly show that the necessities of the grantee, along with those of his family, are determinative of the extent of the privileges and rights to be enjoyed by him under a grant of use and habitation.

notes: No actual boarders were taken in this case; the Civil Code article quoted establishes, as a matter of law, that a resident occupying under even a limited habitation right (not full ownership) may lawfully take in boarders while inhabiting the house herself. characterization left null because no specific letting transaction was classified by the court.

court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit
holding_summary: Plaintiff, a paying hotel guest for several months, sued the hotel operator for property stolen from his locked room. The court held that under the Civil Code articles governing innkeepers, the hotel operator was liable to the paying guest for the loss because it had not complied with statutory prerequisites (safe deposit and posted notices) that would have limited its liability.

quotes.text: An innkeeper' is responsible as depositary for the effects brought by travelers who lodge at his house; the deposit of such effects is considered as a necessary deposit.

We experience no difficulty in reaching the conclusion that under the facts of this case and the law defining the duties and fixing the liability of innkeepers to their paying guests, defendant is responsible to plaintiff for the value of the articles stolen from his room.

notes: Favorable in the sense that the court enforces protections for a paying lodger against the commercial operator; the dispute is over liability for stolen property, not the legality of the letting itself.

court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit
holding_summary: A deed restriction bound the purchaser, her heirs, successors and assigns never to build or permit a 'saloon, nightclub or tourist court' on the conveyed land. The court held this restriction was a real obligation running with the land (distinguishing Le Blanc v. Palmisano, where similar language lacked express successor-binding terms), and thus was binding and enforceable against subsequent owners, barring construction of a tourist court.

quotes.text: And now the said purchaser hereby binds and obligates herself unto the said Edward L. Woodside, never to build or permit the building of any saloon, nightclub or tourist court upon the property herein conveyed.
The restrictive stipulation was not forbidden by law and was binding upon Mrs. Roberts and all subsequent purchasers.

notes: Adverse: court sustains a permanent restriction barring a tourist court (short-term commercial lodging) as a valid, binding real obligation. characterization left null since no actual letting transaction is characterized, only covenant validity.

holding_summary: A laborer who rented a room from a tenant occupying half of a dwelling was injured falling through an unfloored attic space while moving in. The court held the building owner not liable because that portion of the attic was not intended for habitable use, but recognized in its analysis that a sub-occupant renting a room from a tenant may, under the proper facts, recover from the owner for defects even where the tenant could not.

quotes.text: there may be circumstances in which a third person rightfully in the premises as a sublessee of the tenant, or as a guest of-the tenant, may recover from the owner of the building, even though the tenant could-riot have recovered

we find no defect here and no fault in original construction, and therefore, the owner is not liable since the accident resulted either from fault of the tenant in unfastening the door and in permitting the subtenant to use it, or from negligence on the part of the subtenant, himself.

notes: The court treats a tenant's informal renting-out of a spare room to a laborer as an unremarkable, legitimate arrangement (never questioning its legality) while resolving tort liability; characterization left null because the court never doctrinally classified the room arrangement as lease/license/lodging.

court: Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit
holding_summary: Tenants sued their landlord for OPA rent-overcharge damages after the landlord attempted to reclassify an apartment as separately registered 'sleeping rooms' (with kitchen privileges) to obtain a higher combined rent ceiling under the Hotel and Rooming-house Regulation. On rehearing, the court found the landlord had in fact continued to rent the premises as a single apartment to all three tenants, making the sleeping-room registration an unlawful evasion of the price ceiling, and awarded tenants damages and attorney's fees.

quotes.text: she in fact rented the premises as an apartment and did collect a rental in excess of the ceiling fixed
The maximum rent, and other requirements provided in this regulation shall not be evaded, either directly or indirectly, in connection with the renting or leasing

the fact remains that she made no physical changes and she in fact rented the premises to the three plaintiffs and accepted the $75 payments, knowing that the three people, each and all used the premises as an apartment unit.

notes: Directly on point: regulatory scheme (OPA/Hotel and Rooming-house Regulation) governing rental of sleeping rooms with kitchen privileges is enforced against a landlord's evasion attempt, an adverse (regulation-sustained) result for the higher-rent sleeping-room letting scheme.
